rubric.name: Launch post review (strict)
rubric.description: Is this X post ready to go out, and is every claim in it true?
rubric.context:
You review a draft post for X that announces a demo video. The audience is developers and designers who use coding
agents. brief.md lists the only facts the post may use. Judge only the post text. Be strict: when in doubt, judge it
as failing. Each check looks only at the kind of problem it names; ignore other kinds of problems when judging it.

levels.label: flat
levels.description: Opens with an announcement, a greeting or excitement (we just released, big news, excited to share)

levels.label: ok
levels.description: Opens with the topic, but nothing surprising

levels.label: hook
levels.description: The first line alone makes a developer want the next: a concrete surprise, a number or a tension

levels.label: vague
levels.description: Adjectives and promises; you can't tell what the video shows

levels.label: some
levels.description: One concrete detail, the rest general

levels.label: concrete
levels.description: Says what the agent did and what the scores were, with the numbers that matter

levels.label: muddled
levels.description: Several ideas, jargon or clutter crowd it

levels.label: mostly
levels.description: One idea, but wordy or with filler

levels.label: clear
levels.description: One idea a developer gets in one read

criteria.name: Every claim is in the brief

anchors.overclaims: The post claims something brief.md doesn't say, or stretches it: that Verdict or the agent works on any page, fixes things by itself, guarantees a result, or a number or time that isn't in the brief
anchors.true: Every claim about what happened, the scores and the time is in brief.md. Tone, wording and missing things are judged elsewhere

anchors.hype: The post praises itself (insane, mind-blowing, the best, game-changing, wild), shouts in ALL CAPS or uses exclamation marks
anchors.plain: No self-praise, no ALL-CAPS words and no exclamation marks; it says what happened in plain words

anchors.missing: The post doesn't say that Tideline is a fictional product, so a reader could take the demo for a real company's page
anchors.flagged: The post says plainly that Tideline (or the product in the demo) is fictional or made up

anchors.missing: The post names Verdict without saying what kind of tool it is, so a reader who has never heard of it can't tell
anchors.said: The post says in plain words what Verdict is or does: it scores work against a rubric (an evaluation engine)

anchors.missing: The post makes the run sound flawless; it doesn't mention that some rounds barely moved or that a fix was partial
anchors.said: The post says something that didn't go smoothly, from brief.md: two rounds barely moved because the fix was partial

criteria.name: Ends with a question readers can answer

anchors.closed: The post ends without asking readers anything, or asks only for likes, follows or reposts
anchors.asks: The post ends with a specific question developers can answer from their own work

aggregation.formula: claims_true_n < 0.5 ? 0 : (hook_n * 3 + specific_n * 2 + clear_n) / 6 * (1 + no_hype_n + hashtags_n + mentions_n + styled_text_n + fiction_flagged_n + what_it_is_n + limits_n + question_n) / 9

gates.message: Overclaims: the post says something the brief doesn't support

evidence.label: post.md
evidence.text:
An AI one-shot landing page scored 0. Eight minutes later it scored 93. Honestly the most INSANE thing we've built!!!

Claude Code took an AI one-shot landing page for Tideline and rebuilt it one check at a time, scored by Verdict.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀: 0 → 10 → 20 → 23 → 33 → 34 → 49 → 58 → 71 → 93, in about 8 minutes, unattended.

cc @AnthropicAI @github

#AI #DevTools #buildinpublic #webdev #SaaS

evidence.label: brief.md
evidence.text:
# What the post announces (facts the post may use)
- A 29-second screen recording: Claude Code, the landing page it edits, and the page's score with seven checks.
- The landing page is a real AI one-shot. Claude Code was asked: "Build a modern, beautiful SaaS landing page for
  Tideline, an uptime monitoring tool for small engineering teams. ... Make it pop." Tideline is fictional.
- The one-shot had three made-up testimonials, a "used by 2,400+ teams" logo strip of made-up companies, invented
  stats (12 regions, 99.987% uptime), glowing gradients, looping animations, ALL-CAPS section labels, a gradient
  headline word and slogan headings ("before your coffee cools"). Its own summary said the testimonials and stats were
  placeholders.
- Verdict scored it against a rubric built from research on landing pages and AI-slop tells, plus a facts.json of what
  is true about the product:
  - gate: no invented social proof (the FTC's rule bans fake testimonials); failing it scores 0;
  - six checks: every figure comes from facts.json, no glows or gradients, no looping motion, no template chrome,
    WCAG AA contrast, headings that describe instead of sell.
- The agent fixed one failing check per round and re-scored.
- Scores: 0 → 10 → 20 → 23 → 33 → 34 → 49 → 58 → 71 → 93. It passed ("ship it", 85+) on the 10th evaluation, after
  about 8 minutes, unattended. Two rounds barely moved because the fix was partial; measured checks count only at 100%.
- Verdict is an evaluation engine: rubrics scored by decision models, humans and deterministic checks.
- Audience: developers and designers on X who use coding agents.
- The post goes out with the 29-second video attached.
